text:
The river begins as a thread of meltwater high in the pass, where the snow lingers into June and the only sound is wind over stone. By the time it reaches the first village it has gathered a dozen smaller streams, and the farmers there measure the year by its height against the old mill wall: a wet spring brings it to the third course of bricks, a dry one leaves the second exposed and cracking in the sun. Below the mill the water slows, widens, and turns the colour of weak tea as it crosses the peat flats, and herons stand in it for hours without moving. Nobody downstream remembers who built the first weir, but everyone agrees it was a mistake.

The town that grew up at the river's mouth kept its records in a stone house with a slate roof, and for two hundred years the clerks wrote the same things in the same ledgers: tonnage landed, salt sold, fines paid, names of the drowned. The ledgers survive because the house was dull. Nobody thought to burn it in any of the wars, and nobody thought to sell the books when the town's money ran out, so they sat on their shelves gathering a soft grey fur of dust until a schoolteacher with a bad knee and a long winter ahead of her began to read them in order. What she found was not a secret but a rhythm. Every forty years or so the entries thinned, the handwriting changed, and the price of salt doubled; every forty years or so, in other words, the river had moved, and the town had quietly moved with it, a street at a time, without ever writing down that this was what it was doing.

She published her findings in a pamphlet that sold eleven copies. One of them reached an engineer in the capital who was, at that moment, drawing plans for a harbour wall that assumed the river would stay exactly where it was. He read the pamphlet twice, wrote a short and polite letter to the schoolteacher, and then did what engineers usually do with inconvenient history: he built the wall anyway, a little higher, and added a footnote. The wall stood for thirty-eight years. When the river moved, it did so in a single night of rain, and in the morning the harbour was a lake of brown water with the tops of the fishing boats showing through it like the backs of sleeping animals. The schoolteacher was long dead by then. Her pamphlet was reprinted, and this time it sold rather well, mostly to people who wanted to feel that someone had seen it coming.

What the pamphlet could not explain, and what the ledgers never recorded, was why the town had always moved with the river rather than against it. The engineer's successors spent a great deal of money finding out. They dug trenches through the old streets and found, under each one, the ghost of an older street at a slight angle to it, and under that another, and so on down through the centuries until the trenches hit gravel and the river's own bed, which had been there before any of them.
